title: De altitudine columnarum sub proprio pondere corruentium

deep.reconstruction:
Context: E510 treats a vertical uniform cylindrical column buckling under its own weight. Earlier sections reduce the problem to a linear ODE with a variable coefficient, solved by power series. The series sums P, Q (and P', Q') depend on a dimensionless load parameter t, and the critical (buckling) value of t is fixed by the determinant-type condition P(1+Q') = QP'. The previous page summed the alternating series term by term with logarithms for the trial value t = 200, giving P = 0.1734, Q = 2.7284, P' = 0.1631, Q' = 1.4980.

§37: Euler forms P(1+Q') = 0.4331 and QP' = 0.4450. The mismatch, P(1+Q') − QP' = −0.0119, is small and negative. He takes this to mean that t = 200 is very close to the root and slightly above it. He then argues that more precision is pointless, because only t^{1/3} enters the final formula. This is an error-propagation argument: a relative error ε in t gives roughly ε/3 in the height.

§38 (Problem): find, for every cylindrical column, the greatest height it can have before collapsing under its own weight. In the solution he calibrates against a small model column of the same material, with height a and cross-section dd, that safely carries λ times its own weight.

Next page: the result is h = a·∛(λ·bb·t/(π²·dd)) for a column of section bb. With t = 200, ∛(t/π²) = 2.7263. Euler rounds this down to e = 2.71828 (merely as a convenient constant) and then to 2.70. The modern content is:
- the critical height scales as (EI/q)^{1/3};
- for geometrically similar sections this means h ∝ (cross-sectional area)^{1/3}, i.e. h ∝ diameter^{2/3}.
errors: The final eigenvalue t ≈ 200 does not agree with the modern solution of the self-weight buckling problem. Greenhill (1881), using Bessel functions, found q·L³/EI ≈ 7.837 for a column clamped at the base and free at the top. With Euler's normalisation via π² (pinned reference column), the correct t would be about 7.84 instead of 200; with a cantilever reference (π²/4) it would be about 31.3. Either way the coefficient 2.72 is far too large: the correct value is about 0.93 or 1.46 respectively. So Euler's numerical constant is erroneous, consistent with the standard historical verdict that his treatment in E510 failed to give the right critical value. The exact source of the error lies in earlier sections (equation or boundary conditions) not visible here; unsure.

Gap: the claim that a negative mismatch implies t is slightly too large is asserted without checking monotonicity. Only one trial value is computed on this page, so the direction of correction is not justified.
Replacing 2.7263 by e is numerically arbitrary. The 'h = 2,70 ∛(...)' on the next page omits the factor a (a typo/slip).

ideas.what: Critical value of the load parameter determined by a sign change/mismatch of a characteristic combination of power-series sums (a shooting/secular-equation approach).
ideas.modern_name: Eigenvalue of a boundary-value problem via a characteristic equation solved by trial (series solution of a Bessel/Airy-type equation)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Greenhill 1881 (Bessel-function solution of the self-weight column)
ideas.where_published: E510 itself (Acta Acad. Sci. Petrop. 1778:I, publ. 1780); Opera omnia II.17

ideas.what: Error-propagation argument: since only the cube root of t enters, an error in t is damped threefold.
Scaling law for the maximal self-supporting height, h ∝ (λ·area)^{1/3}, calibrated by a model test (λ from a small column of the same material).
ideas.modern_name: Greenhill's height law h ∝ (EI/ρgA)^{1/3}, giving h ∝ d^{2/3}; model similitude
ideas.where_published: E510; discussed in Truesdell's history of elastic bodies (Opera omnia II.11/2)

missed.claim: Euler derives the correct dimensional scaling for self-weight buckling, h ∝ (λ bb/dd)^{1/3}, i.e. height ∝ diameter^{2/3} for similar sections, though his numerical constant is wrong. The 2/3-power law is commonly attributed to Greenhill (1881) and in allometry to McMahon (1973), with Euler at most mentioned as having failed. This is known to Euler historians (Truesdell), so it is only marginally 'missed'.
missed.quote: maximam altitudinem quaesitam esse h = a∛(λbb/(ππdd)·t)
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: Priority note for the elastic-similarity scaling used in tree and organism allometry; it separates Euler's correct scaling from his incorrect eigenvalue.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a routine numerical conclusion of a known (and known-to-be-flawed) Euler paper on self-weight buckling. The cube-root scaling is correct, but the constant (t ≈ 200) is wrong, and both facts are in the standard history.
transcription_corrections: Transcription matches the image; no substantive corrections. (Next page: 'h = 2,70∛(λbb/dd)' lacks the factor a in the original print itself.)
